items.summary: Learn how the PL-300 exam works and how to answer its question styles, sit your first PL-300 timed set, start an error journal, review high-yield decision rules across all four skill areas, and set up the continual-improvement register for the analytics service.

read.heading: How the PL-300 exam works
read.body:
Facts to plan around:

- Certification: Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate, exam PL-300.
- Time: 100 minutes. Passing score: 700 on a scaled score. A scaled score is not a percentage, so do not try to count marks as you go.
- Microsoft does not publish a fixed number of questions. Note the count on the start screen and set checkpoints, for example a third of the questions done by a third of the time.
- Skill areas: Prepare the data 25–30%; Model the data 25–30%; Visualize and analyze the data 25–30%; Manage and secure Power BI 15–20%.
- Delivery: proctored through Pearson VUE. The exam may include interactive components.
- A failed first attempt can be retaken after 24 hours. The certification renews every 12 months with a free online assessment.

Expect several formats. Some items ask for one or more answers. Some give a Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) or Power Query snippet with drop-down blanks to complete. Some ask you to put steps in order. A case study gives a longer business scenario, often split into tabs such as background, requirements and existing environment, followed by several questions.

Some sections may not let you return once you leave them, and the exam tells you on screen when that applies. Read those screens, and make every change you want in a section before you move on.

read.heading: Answering PL-300 questions
read.body:
Most PL-300 questions are a requirement plus constraints. Find both:

1. Read the last sentence first. It says what you must do: create, configure, reduce, ensure.
2. Mark the constraints: "minimize development effort", "users must see only their region", "without changing the semantic model", "data must be no more than 15 minutes old". The constraint usually decides between two answers that would both work.
3. Eliminate answers that work but break a constraint. Bidirectional filtering might fix a total, but not if the question says to avoid ambiguity.
4. For DAX drop-downs, check what each function needs: CALCULATE takes an expression, then filters; DIVIDE takes a numerator, a denominator and an optional alternate result; USERELATIONSHIP sits inside CALCULATE.
5. For ordering items, picture the screen. You cannot mark a date table before the date column exists, and you cannot add role members in the service before you publish.
6. For a case study, read the requirements first, then each question, then go back to the background for the detail that question needs.

Pacing: do not spend more than about twice your average time on one item. Give your best answer, mark it for review if the exam allows, and move on.

read.heading: Timed sets and the error journal
read.body:
In TriCert Lab, Practice, Timed set gives you 15 minutes of questions for the exam you choose and records the result as evidence. Choose PL-300. The exam gate needs two timed sets at 80% or better for PL-300 and two for ITIL, so today is your first PL-300 attempt.

Run it like the real exam: no notes, no pausing, answer in order. When you are unsure, mark the answer as a guess. A guessed answer lands in Practice, Review even if it was right, which is what you want, because a lucky answer is not knowledge.

Afterwards open Review. It holds every wrong or guessed answer, linked to the document that teaches it. Keep an error journal entry for each:

1. Restate the scenario in one line.
2. Name the rule or principle that decides it.
3. Say why your answer failed: a misread constraint, a wrong fact, or the weaker of two plausible answers.
4. Write the trigger words you will recognize next time.
5. Open the linked document, fix your understanding there, and put it in Explain it in your own words.

A wrong answer stays open until you answer that question correctly again. Gate check 5 needs no open wrong answers and at least six written explanations of 80 characters or more, and the journal is how you get there.

Look for patterns: three misses on filter context are one topic to repair.

read.heading: High-yield PL-300: prepare and model
read.body:
Decision rules to know cold:

- Import for speed and full features; DirectQuery when data must be current or is too large to import; Direct Lake for Delta tables in Fabric OneLake.
- A gateway is needed for on-premises or private-network sources, not for cloud sources the service can reach.
- Profile the entire data set, not the default first 1,000 rows, before declaring data clean.
- Replace or remove errors only under a recorded rule, and keep rejected rows as evidence (Kestrel rule DQ-13).
- Set data types before loading; numbers stored as text break sums and sorting.
- Fact tables hold events at one grain; dimensions hold descriptions. Relate them on keys, one-to-many, single direction.
- Mark a contiguous date table for classic time intelligence, and turn off Auto date/time.
- A measure responds to filter context; a calculated column is fixed at refresh.
- CALCULATE changes filter context. REMOVEFILTERS or ALL clears filters, for example to get a share of a total.
- Semi-additive values add across units but not across days: 12,952 staffed bed-days is not 144 beds.
- Use DIVIDE for ratios so a zero denominator returns blank instead of an error.
- Use Performance Analyzer to find slow visuals and DAX query view to run and test their queries.
- Shrink the model: remove unused columns, lower cardinality, reduce granularity.

read.heading: High-yield PL-300: visualize and manage
read.body:
- The visual follows the question: compare (bar), trend (line), relationship (scatter), one value against a goal (a card, or a KPI visual: key performance indicator).
- Conditional formatting by rules, gradient or field value; field value lets a measure supply the colour.
- The drillthrough field goes on the target page; Keep all filters carries the source page's filters.
- Turn off a bookmark's Data option when it must not reset filters.
- Sync slicers: sync applies the selection; visible shows the slicer.
- Report page tooltip: Allow use as tooltip on the page, and Type Report page on the visual.
- Accessibility: alt text, tab order, contrast, never colour alone, a table alternative.
- Paginated reports for print, PDF and every row; interactive reports for exploration.
- Workspace roles: Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer. Row-level security (RLS) filters Viewers and app users only.
- Static RLS has a fixed filter per role, such as DimSite[SiteCode] = "KGH" (Kestrel General Hospital). Dynamic RLS filters a security table with USERPRINCIPALNAME (), so one role serves every site.
- Assign RLS role members, preferably groups, in the service after publishing; test with View as and Test as role.
- Apps: audiences control content; Update app releases report changes.
- Sensitivity labels apply to items and follow exports; endorsement is Promoted or Certified.
- Build permission lets people create content on a semantic model.

read.heading: The continual-improvement register
read.body:
Now the ITIL part of the session. Continual improvement is one of the five components of the ITIL Value System, with the guiding principles, governance, value chain activities and management practices. ITIL 4 framed it as seven questions, and Version 5 refines that model. The questions still work as prompts:

1. What is the vision?
2. Where are we now?
3. Where do we want to be?
4. How do we get there?
5. Take action.
6. Did we get there?
7. How do we keep the momentum going?

A continual-improvement register (CIR) holds every improvement idea in one place so ideas are compared, prioritized and followed through. Each entry needs an ID, the idea, its source, the value it would create, a baseline and a target, a priority, an owner and a status.

Beacon's first entries come from evidence you already hold. In August and September 2026 the service desk logged 27 tickets in the Power BI category. The 6 that were access requests met their resolution target only once (16.7%), with a median of 105.5 hours. That is a strong candidate: grant dashboard access through Identity Directory groups mapped to app audiences, which Release 2 will automate. Other sources are the known errors from go-live (a missing census day should raise an alert, not a call) and yesterday's lessons.

Prioritize by value against effort, and start where you are.

keyTerms.definition: A score converted to a fixed scale, such as PL-300's pass mark of 700. It is not a percentage of questions correct, so counting marks during the exam is pointless.
A PL-300 item type with a longer business scenario, often in tabs such as background and requirements, followed by several questions that depend on it.
A record of each wrong or guessed answer: the scenario, the deciding rule, why your answer failed, and trigger words, with the fix written into the linked document.
Row-level security where one role filters a security table by the signed-in user, using USERPRINCIPALNAME (), instead of one fixed role per site or region.
A single list of improvement ideas, each with source, value, baseline, target, priority, owner and status, so ideas are compared and followed through.
The ITIL 4 model that Version 5 refines: vision, where are we now, where do we want to be, how do we get there, take action, did we get there, keep the momentum.

examTips.tip: Find the constraint before choosing: 'minimize effort', 'without changing the model', 'only their region'. Two options usually work; the constraint decides which one is right.
Dynamic RLS uses one role whose filter compares a security table's email column with USERPRINCIPALNAME (). Static RLS needs a separate role for every site or region.
Continual improvement is a component of the ITIL Value System. The seven questions, from ITIL 4 and refined in Version 5, begin with the vision and the current state before any action.
Start where you are: measure the current service before replacing anything. Questions that jump straight to a new tool or full redesign usually ignore this principle.

pitfalls: Retaking a timed set straight away to reach 80% from memory, which proves recall of those questions, not readiness.
Answering without marking guesses, so lucky answers never reach Review.
Filling the improvement register with ideas that have no baseline, owner or measure.
Studying only the skill area you enjoy. The weights are close, so every area matters.

check.q: Users must see only their region, and the solution must need little maintenance as regions are added. Static or dynamic RLS?
check.a: Dynamic RLS. One role filters a security table by USERPRINCIPALNAME (), so adding a region means adding rows to that table, not creating roles. Static RLS needs a new role and new membership for every region, which breaks the maintenance constraint.

check.q: You scored 85% on your first PL-300 timed set but marked four answers as guesses. Are you finished with them?
check.a: No. Guessed answers go to Review even when right, because luck is not knowledge. Journal each one, fix your understanding in the linked document, and answer it again. The gate also needs a second PL-300 timed set at 80% or better.

check.q: Why is the Power BI access-request entry a good continual-improvement item?
check.a: It has a measured baseline (6 requests in August and September, 1 within target, 16.7%, median 105.5 hours), a clear outcome for leaders (access to their site on day one), a feasible approach (groups mapped to app audiences and RLS) and an owner. It also links to Release 2, so it will be delivered rather than parked.

items.summary: Learn how the ITIL Foundation (Version 5) exam works and review its high-yield content, sit your second PL-300 timed set and your first ITIL set, cover the remaining PL-300 topics Beacon did not exercise, and run the first service review of the analytics service.

read.heading: How the ITIL Foundation (Version 5) exam works
read.body:
- 40 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. Pass mark 65%, which is 26 of 40.
- Closed book. Online proctored delivery is available, and no training course is required first.
- The certificate renews every 3 years, through continuing professional development or a retake.

That is 90 seconds a question. Plan one pass through all 40 in about 45 minutes, then use the last 15 on the questions you marked.

Questions test definitions and how they apply:

1. Read the stem twice and find the key word: value, outcome, output, utility, warranty, principle, dimension, stage.
2. Watch for negatives. "Which is NOT" and "which is LEAST likely" reverse the task.
3. Eliminate answers that are true but answer a different question.
4. Prefer the answer about value for the consumer over the one about internal activity.
5. Answer every question; a blank cannot score.

The learning objectives cover product and service management concepts, value co-creation, the four dimensions, the Value System, the guiding principles, the lifecycle, management practices, continual improvement, and value stream mapping and management. Version 5 builds artificial intelligence (AI) use and governance in throughout and is described as AI-native, so expect AI across topics.

read.heading: High-yield ITIL: value, roles and the guiding principles
read.body:
Core ideas, with the Beacon analytics service as the example:

- Value is co-created by provider and consumer. The dashboards create value only when leaders use them to act.
- An output is what an activity produces (a report page). An outcome is the result a stakeholder wants (leaders acting earlier on bed pressure).
- Utility is fit for purpose: what the service does (shows waits and occupancy by site). Warranty is fit for use: how well it does it (available, current, secure, recoverable). Value needs both.
- Roles: the customer defines requirements and owns outcomes (Janelle Cardinal); the user uses the service (a charge nurse); the sponsor authorizes budget (Dr. Helen Marchetti).

The ITIL Value System has five components: guiding principles, governance, value chain activities, management practices and continual improvement.

| Guiding principle | Beacon example |
|---|---|
| Focus on value | Count decisions made, not pages built |
| Start where you are | Baseline tickets before redesign |
| Progress iteratively with feedback | Pilot pages with one site |
| Collaborate and promote visibility | Desk co-writes knowledge |
| Think and work holistically | Refresh, gateway, security and desk as one service |
| Keep it simple and practical | Three support tiers |
| Optimize and automate | Simplify access first, then automate |

read.heading: High-yield ITIL: dimensions, lifecycle and practices
read.body:
The four dimensions of product and service management must all be considered for every service:

- Organizations and People: roles, skills, culture (Tomás Rivera's key-person risk).
- Information and Technology: data, tools and platforms (the semantic model, the gateway, the warehouse A-010).
- Partners and Suppliers: other organizations involved (Lumen Analytics Partners; Microsoft as the Power BI provider).
- Value Streams and Processes: how work flows to create value (a request for dashboard access, end to end).

Version 5 organizes work around an eight-stage product and service lifecycle, which replaces ITIL 4's service value chain as the organizing model:

| Stage | For the analytics service |
|---|---|
| Discover | Leaders' pain with emailed extracts |
| Design | Pages, measures, security, service levels |
| Acquire | Lumen contract; Power BI capacity |
| Build | Semantic model, reports, tests |
| Transition | Go-live decision D-02 and handover |
| Operate | Refresh, gateway and workspaces monitored and maintained |
| Deliver | Access requests handled; reports used each morning; feedback collected |
| Support | Incidents and problems resolved, using known errors and workarounds |

Management practices are sets of organizational resources for a type of work, such as incident, problem and service level management; Version 5 keeps them with adjustments and new groupings. A value stream is the series of steps that turns demand into value; mapping it shows where work waits.

read.heading: PL-300 topics Beacon did not exercise
read.body:
- Analyze: right-click a data point and choose Analyze to explain an increase or decrease, or to find where a distribution differs.
- Grouping and binning: group selected data points, or bin a numeric field into equal ranges. MinutesToPIA in 30-minute bins makes a wait histogram.
- Clustering: on a scatter chart, Automatically find clusters groups similar points.
- AI visuals: Key influencers ranks factors that drive an outcome; Decomposition tree breaks a measure down by dimensions in any order; Q&A answers typed questions.
- Analytics pane: constant, average, median and percentile lines; trend lines; error bars; forecasting on a line chart with a continuous date axis; Find anomalies on a line chart.
- Copilot, where allowed: a narrative visual, a new report page from a prompt, suggestions, and a semantic model summary.
- Personalize visuals lets viewers change a visual's type or fields for themselves.
- Export settings decide whether users can export summarized data, underlying data, or nothing.
- Automatic page refresh updates visuals at a fixed interval or on change detection, for DirectQuery sources.
- Dashboards: one canvas in the service built by pinning tiles from reports.
- Data alerts: set on dashboard tiles pinned from cards, KPIs and gauges; they notify when a value crosses a threshold. Alerts on report visuals use a separate Fabric feature, Activator.
- Subscriptions email a snapshot of a report page or dashboard on a schedule.
- Item access: share with Read, Reshare or Build. Add security groups, not individuals, to row-level security roles in the service.

read.heading: The first service review
read.body:
A service review checks with the customer whether the service delivers what was agreed and what it is worth; it belongs to service level management. Grace Liu (E-005), the service owner, chairs it. Attendees: Janelle Cardinal (E-008), business owner; Tomás Rivera (E-006); Mei Tanaka (E-013); Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007); and you. Agenda: service levels, experience, outcomes, incidents and known errors, changes, improvements, actions.

The service has only just gone live, so this first review sets the baseline from the Power BI tickets of August and September 2026. The figures below were computed from khn_service_desk.csv with Kestrel's cleaning rules. "Met target" means resolved within the priority's resolution target (P1 4 hours, P2 8, P3 24, P4 72).

| Measure | Power BI tickets | All tickets |
|---|---|---|
| Tickets | 27 (13 incidents, 8 service requests, 6 access requests) | 219 |
| Incidents met target | 66.7% (8 of 12) | 76.4% |
| Service requests met target | 50.0% (4 of 8) | 82.1% |
| Access requests met target | 16.7% (1 of 6) | 15.2% |
| Median incident hours | 12.0 | 14.4 |
| Satisfaction (1 to 5) | 3.0 from 9 responses | 3.5 from 88 |

Three readings. Power BI service requests miss target far more often than the desk average. Nine satisfaction responses are too few to trust, so collecting more is an action. And targets can look green while leaders still email extracts: the watermelon effect, green outside and red inside. So from go-live the review also tracks app usage by site and the charter measures.

read.heading: Update the catalogue entry and service levels
read.body:
The review ends by updating the service catalogue entry and its service levels so the agreement reflects what you learned:

- Add the measures the review showed you need: Power BI service requests resolved within target, dashboard access granted within target, and refresh completed by the agreed time.
- Separate warranty measures (refresh success, availability, row-level security defects) from experience measures (satisfaction, time to get access) and outcome measures (leaders using the app each week, and the charter measures in January 2027).
- Put the baseline beside every target, and mark targets as proposed until Janelle Cardinal agrees them.
- Keep the review rhythm monthly, with the business owner and the service owner, and record the date of the next review.
- Copy every gap into the continual-improvement register with an owner.

Then sit your second PL-300 timed set and an ITIL timed set, and journal every miss. Two PL-300 sets at 80% or better meet the PL-300 part of gate check 3; ITIL needs two of its own.

keyTerms.definition: Fit for purpose: what a product or service does to meet a need, such as showing waits and occupancy by site.
Fit for use: assurance that a service meets agreed requirements for things like availability, capacity, security and continuity, such as refresh that survives a server patch.
An output is something an activity produces, such as a report page. An outcome is a result a stakeholder wants, such as acting earlier on bed pressure.
A regular meeting with the customer to check performance against service levels, experience, outcomes, incidents, changes and improvements, ending in owned actions.
Service measures that look green while the customer's experience or outcomes are poor. It is avoided by measuring use, satisfaction and outcomes, not only targets met.
ITIL Version 5's eight stages: Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver and Support, the organizing model in place of ITIL 4's value chain.

build.goal: Run the first service review of the analytics service with baseline ticket figures, update the Service catalogue entry and service levels, and complete your second PL-300 timed set and a first ITIL timed set.

Enter the Power BI baseline table (27 tickets; 66.7%, 50.0% and 16.7% met target by type; median 12.0 incident hours; satisfaction 3.0 from 9) beside the all-ticket figures.
Write three findings, including the small satisfaction sample and the watermelon risk, and the use and outcome measures you will add from go-live.
Update the service levels: separate warranty, experience and outcome measures, show each baseline, and mark unagreed targets as proposed.
Record actions with owners and dates and copy each into the Continual-improvement register; tick Done when and write your explanation.
Open Practice, Timed set: complete your second PL-300 set, then an ITIL set. Journal every wrong or guessed answer in Review.
build.modelAnswer: Service review 1 (example extract). Attendees: Janelle Cardinal, Grace Liu, Tomás Rivera, Mei Tanaka, Dr. Sarah Whitford, Programme Manager. Finding 1: Power BI service requests met target 50.0% (4 of 8) against 82.1% for all service requests. Action: request template and knowledge article for report changes; owner Mei Tanaka (E-013). Finding 2: only 9 satisfaction responses. Action: one-question survey on every Power BI ticket; owner Grace Liu. Finding 3: no usage data yet. examTips.tip: Utility is fit for purpose and warranty is fit for use; value needs both. A question about availability, capacity, security or continuity is asking about warranty.
Outputs are things produced; outcomes are results stakeholders want. When the options mix them, the ITIL answer usually points to the outcome.
Know the eight lifecycle stages in order: Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver, Support. Do not answer with ITIL 4 value chain activity names.

Power BI data alerts are set on dashboard tiles pinned from cards, KPIs and gauges; alerts on report visuals use Fabric Activator instead. Subscriptions send scheduled snapshots of report pages or dashboards by email.

pitfalls: Treating green service levels as proof of value without checking use and outcomes.
Drawing conclusions from 9 satisfaction responses as if they were representative.
Studying ITIL with ITIL 4 value chain names; the Version 5 exam is organized around the eight-stage lifecycle.
Presenting the August and September figures as post-go-live performance. They are the baseline before the new service.

check.q: Is 'the gateway cluster has two members so refresh survives a server patch' utility or warranty?
check.a: Warranty. It is about how reliably the service performs (availability and continuity), not what it does. Utility is what the dashboards show: waits, occupancy and alternate level of care (ALC) days by site.

check.q: Power BI incidents met target 66.7% of the time with a 12.0-hour median. Does that mean the service is good?
check.a: Not on its own. It covers 12 incidents with a known outcome, before go-live. Service requests met target only 50.0%, satisfaction is 3.0 from just 9 responses, and use has not been measured. Green targets with low use would be the watermelon effect, so the review also tracks usage and outcomes.

check.q: In which lifecycle stage does go-live decision D-02 sit, and which stages follow it?
check.a: Transition. After it the analytics service runs in Operate (refresh, gateway and workspaces monitored and maintained), Deliver (access requests handled and reports used each morning) and Support (incidents and problems resolved by the service desk).

items.summary: Today is the exam gate for PL-300 and ITIL Foundation (Version 5). You read the five gate checks in Progress, decide on evidence whether to sit, follow a simple final-day routine, and record a gate decision. If a check is not met, you do not sit: you repair and rebook.

read.heading: What the gate is for
read.body:
A gate replaces a feeling with evidence. How ready you feel on the morning of an exam depends on sleep and nerves as much as on knowledge. The gate asks two plainer questions: have you done the work, and do your recent answers show you can apply it under time?

This gate closes Release 1 and covers two exams: PL-300 (Microsoft Power BI Data Analyst) and ITIL Foundation (Version 5). Its scope is everything before today: the 28 sessions from week 1 day 1 to week 6 day 3, the 28 Release 1 documents, and your practice for both exams.

The rule is simple: sit an exam only when all five checks are met. If one is not, the honest decision is to repair and rebook, and to write down why. That is not failure. It is the same go or no-go discipline you used for Release 1 on 2026-10-23, applied to yourself.

Gate days also test planning. If you booked the exams for today, check the booking rules for moving a date well before the cut-off they give, so a missed check costs you a new date rather than an attempt.

read.heading: Reading the five checks in Progress
read.body:
Open Progress. Beside the four readiness scores (coverage 30, documents 35, judgment 25, recall 10), the next exam gate lists five checks:

| Check | What it needs | If not met |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Every session before the gate done (28 of 28) | Open Today, finish each missing session, Mark done |
| 2 | Every document in the releases up to the gate complete (28 of 28) | In Project, finish the Done when list of each incomplete document |
| 3 | Two timed sets at 80% or better for each exam | Practice, Timed set; study the misses between attempts |
| 4 | At least 24 decisions for each exam, under 30% wrong | Practice, Scenarios for that exam, weakest topic first |
| 5 | No open wrong answers, and at least 6 written explanations of 80 characters or more | Practice, Review; write explanations in Explain it in your own words |

Read checks 3 and 4 per exam: a PL-300 result does not count for ITIL. Check 4 uses your latest answer to each question, so an old miss you have since answered correctly no longer counts against you. Check 5 counts across both exams, so one open ITIL wrong answer blocks the whole gate.

Do not game the checks. Repeating a timed set until the same questions come out at 80% shows memory, not readiness. Space your attempts and study between them.

read.heading: The final day before you sit
read.body:
Keep the last day light and routine:

1. Run the five checks first thing. If any is not met, stop and go to the repair plan.
2. Review; do not learn new material. Spend 20 to 30 minutes in Practice, Flashcards filtered to PL-300, then the same for ITIL. New topics today add anxiety, not marks.
3. Re-read your error journal: the trigger words and the rules, not the questions themselves.
4. Prepare logistics: the identification your booking asks for, the exact start time, and for online proctoring a quiet room, a clear desk and a computer that has passed the system check beforehand.
5. Plan the order. If you sit both on one day, a sensible plan is PL-300 first, as the longer and more applied exam, with a real break before ITIL.
6. Eat, drink water, and arrive or log in early. Rushing costs more focus than any one topic.

read.heading: In the exam room
read.body:
PL-300 (100 minutes, passing score 700 on a scaled score):

- Note the number of questions on the start screen and set checkpoints at about a third and two thirds of the time, leaving time to review.
- Read the requirement and the constraint before the options.
- In a case study, read the requirements first. Make every change you want before leaving any section the exam says cannot be revisited.
- If an item takes more than twice your average time, choose your best answer, mark it if allowed, and move on.

ITIL Foundation (40 questions, 60 minutes, 26 correct to pass):

- First pass in about 45 minutes; the last 15 for marked questions.
- Find the key word in each stem: value, outcome, utility, warranty, principle, dimension, stage.
- Watch for NOT and LEAST.
- Answer all 40.

In both: a run of hard questions does not mean you are failing. Breathe out slowly, reset, and treat the next question as the first. Do not change an answer on review unless you can name the rule that makes the new one right.

read.heading: If a check fails, or an exam does
read.body:
If a check is not met, do not sit. Write a repair plan in the same shape as a go-live condition: what is missing, the action, the evidence that will close it, and a date.

| Failed check | Repair |
|---|---|
| 1 or 2 | Finish the work; usually hours, not weeks |
| 3 | A day or two on the topics behind the misses, then a new timed set |
| 4 | Practice, Scenarios for the weak exam until 24 decisions with under 30% wrong |
| 5 | Clear Review, then write the missing explanations in your documents |

Rebook only when the plan's evidence is in place.

If you sit an exam and do not pass, use the score report, which shows how you did in each skill area. Map each weak area to the Beacon documents in your coverage review and repair those first. You may retake PL-300 24 hours after a first failed attempt, but retaking once the repair work is done is wiser than retaking the next day. For ITIL, take the same approach through its learning objectives.

Either way, Beacon continues tomorrow with Release 2. Keep the next session on schedule and fit repair work around it, as a programme keeps delivering while it fixes a defect.

read.heading: Record the gate decision
read.body:
Record the gate decision as you would any programme decision: date, scope, each check with the value Progress shows, the decision for each exam, the pacing plan and the next action. Write it before you sit, while the evidence is in front of you, and add the result afterwards.

A good record lets someone else see exactly why you sat or did not. It also sets the pattern for the later gates: the PMP gate at week 10 day 3 and the CISSP gate at week 13 day 4 use the same five checks.

If a check changes during the day, for example you clear two open wrong answers in the morning, record both readings and what you did in between. That shows the decision followed the evidence, not the other way round.

The model answer below is a filled record for PL-300 and ITIL. Every value in it is an example to show the format. Use your own numbers from Progress, and never copy the example's results into your own record.

keyTerms.definition: A decision point after each release where you sit the release's exams only if all five checks in Progress are met; otherwise you repair and rebook.
Practice, Timed set in TriCert Lab: 15 minutes of questions for the exam you choose, recorded as evidence. The gate needs two at 80% or better per exam.
Your latest recorded answer to a practice question. Check 4 needs at least 24 decisions per exam with under 30% wrong.
A question whose latest answer is wrong. It closes when you answer that question correctly again; check 5 needs none open.
Text of at least 80 characters in a document's Explain it in your own words box. Check 5 needs at least six.
For a failed check: what is missing, the action, the evidence that will close it, and a date, written before you rebook.

build.goal: Apply the five gate checks for PL-300 and ITIL, record a gate decision with evidence, then sit the exams only if every check is met, or write a dated repair plan if any is not.
steps: Open Progress and read the five checks for the PL-300 and ITIL V5 gate. Copy each check's detail into your gate record exactly as shown.
For any check not met, stop and write the repair action, the evidence that will close it, and a date. Do not sit.
If every check is met, run the final-day routine: 20 to 30 minutes of Flashcards per exam, your error journal, then logistics.
Sit PL-300 with the checkpoint pacing plan, take a real break, then sit ITIL with the 45 plus 15 minute plan.
After each exam, record the result and, for any exam not passed, the weak areas from the score report mapped to Beacon documents.
Mark the session done in Today, whatever the result, so Release 2 starts on schedule tomorrow.

Example gate decision record. Every value below is an example to show the format; use your own numbers from Progress.

Gate: PL-300 and ITIL Foundation (Version 5), end of Release 1. Date: week 6, day 4. Decided by: the learner.

| Check (as named in Progress) | Shown in Progress (example) | Met |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Sessions before the gate done | 28 of 28 sessions | Yes |
| 2. Release documents complete | 28 of 28 documents in Release 1 | Yes |
| 3. Two timed sets at 80% or better | PL-300 2 of 2, ITIL V5 2 of 2 (example scores 82%, 86%; 80%, 88%) | Yes |
| 4. No major weak area | PL-300 41 of 24 decisions, 17% wrong; ITIL V5 30 of 24 decisions, 23% wrong | Yes |
| 5. Mistakes reviewed and explained | 0 wrong answers open, 9 of 6 explanations | Yes, after re-check |

Re-check (example): at 08:00, check 5 showed 2 wrong answers open, both ITIL (utility against warranty, and the Transition stage). Both were journalled, the linked documents updated, and both questions answered correctly at 09:10. Check 5 then showed 0 open.

Weakest topics from the error journal (example): PL-300 calculation groups and data alerts; ITIL utility against warranty.

Decision: sit PL-300 at 13:00 and ITIL at 15:30 (example times) with a 30-minute break.

Pacing plan: PL-300 checkpoints at about 33 and 66 minutes, review from 90 to 100. ITIL first pass by 45 minutes, marked questions to 60.

Result (example): PL-300 passed; ITIL passed. Next action: start Release 2 tomorrow with the current-state access map.

If either had not passed: record the weak PL-300 skill areas from the score report, or the ITIL learning objectives behind your journalled misses, map them to Beacon documents, plan two repair sessions alongside Release 2, and rebook after a new timed set at 80% or better.

examTips.tip: With no published question count, pace from the count on your start screen with checkpoints at thirds. Make every change in a section before leaving it if the exam warns it cannot be revisited.
40 questions in 60 minutes is 90 seconds each, and 26 correct passes. Make one full pass first, return to marked questions, and answer every item.
A failed first attempt can be retaken after 24 hours. Use the skill-area results on the score report to target repair before rebooking rather than retaking straight away.

pitfalls: Sitting because the booking is today even though a check is not met.
Cramming new topics on gate day instead of reviewing the error journal.
Counting a PL-300 timed set toward ITIL; checks 3 and 4 are read per exam.
Changing answers on review without a rule that makes the new answer right.

check.q: Check 3 shows PL-300 2 of 2 and ITIL V5 1 of 2. What do you do?
check.a: The gate is not met, so you do not sit today. Study the topics behind your ITIL misses, sit another ITIL timed set on a later day, and rebook when it scores 80% or better and every other check is still met. Record the decision, the repair action and its date.

check.q: Check 5 shows 1 wrong answer open and 7 of 6 explanations. How do you close it?
check.a: Open Practice, Review, journal the wrong answer (scenario, rule, why it failed, trigger words), fix your understanding in the linked document, and answer that question correctly again. Your latest answer then counts as right, and the open count drops to 0.

check.q: How should you split your time in the ITIL Foundation exam?
check.a: 40 questions in 60 minutes is 90 seconds each. Make one full pass in about 45 minutes, marking uncertain questions, then spend the last 15 minutes on the marked ones. Answer all 40; 26 correct is the pass mark.

items.summary: Release 2 begins. You map how clinicians get and lose access today from the identity, service desk and access review data: where requests wait (median 4.26 days, 27.3% within 72 hours), where control fails (missed leavers E-014 and E-027), and why Kevin Park's combined rights are a segregation-of-duties conflict.

read.heading: Start Release 2 with today's process
read.body:
Release 2, clinician identity and access, runs to its acceptance gate on 2026-11-26. Its charter targets are concrete (baselines from data, targets agreed): access requests resolved within 72 hours from 27.3% to 80%; median days to fulfil from 4.26 to 1; missed leavers from 2 to 0; privileged accounts with multifactor authentication (MFA) from 66.7% to 100%; Q3 access reviews on time from 66.7% to 100%.

You cannot redesign a process you have not seen. A current-state map shows how access is really requested, approved, granted and removed, how long it takes, and where controls fail. It is Release 2's baseline, and it stops the team designing for a process that exists only in a policy.

This is the ITIL guiding principle Start where you are, and the first step of value stream mapping. In CISSP terms it is Domain 5, Identity and Access Management (IAM), and the identity and access provisioning lifecycle: grant, review, change and remove.

One privacy point before you open the files. khn_identity.csv holds staff personal information, not patient health information. For a custodian like Kestrel, staff records fall under the Protection of Privacy Act (POPA), not the Health Information Act. The data dictionary classifies most identity fields Confidential (only job role, department, site and worker type are Internal), so handle the files as Confidential.

read.heading: What the sources prove
read.body:
Each file proves something different. Use them together, as of 2026-10-01:

| Source | What it shows | Key figures |
|---|---|---|
| khn_identity.csv | Accounts, human resources (HR) status, worker type, privilege, MFA | 42 workers, 40 enabled; 2 missed leavers; 6 enabled privileged accounts, 2 without MFA; MFA on 42.5% of enabled accounts |
| khn_service_desk.csv | How long access requests take | 49 access requests, 44 resolved; median 4.26 days (102.3 hours); 27.3% within 72 hours; target met 15.2% |
| khn_access_reviews.csv | Whether managers confirm access | 24 items; 18 due by 2026-09-30, 12 validly done (66.7%), 6 overdue |
| khn_user_permissions.csv | Who holds what, and who granted it | 171 grants; 8 excess grants; 62.6% granted by Kevin Park (E-009) |

An excess grant is a permission the worker's current role does not include.

Profile these files as you did the emergency data. Use each worker's latest row only: E-028 has two overlapping current rows. Treat odd values as findings, not noise: E-031's privileged flag says "Maybe", and E-037's manager, E-099, does not exist.

read.heading: The joiner path: where requests wait
read.body:
A joiner request today, as the tickets show it:

| Step | Who | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Request raised | Manager or clinician | 26 by phone, 16 by portal, 7 walk-up |
| 2. Logged as an access request | Service desk | All 49 go to Identity and Access |
| 3. Approval | Someone with approve access rights | No approval time in the data |
| 4. Account and permissions created | Mostly Kevin Park | 107 of 171 grants made by E-009 |
| 5. Ticket resolved | Identity and Access | Median 102.3 hours |

Requests carry priority P3 (17) or P4 (32), with resolution targets of 24 and 72 hours. Only 7 of the 46 with a known outcome met their target (15.2%). By channel, phone requests met it 28.0% of the time (7 of 25); portal (0 of 16) and walk-up (0 of 5) never did. The longest resolved request took 13.4 days, and 3 of the 49 (6.1%) were reopened.

Be honest about what the data cannot show. Tickets hold only opened and resolved times, so they cannot tell you how much of the 4.26 days is waiting and how much is work. Mark steps 3 and 4 "to be timed" and fill them from a sample of real requests and short interviews with the service desk (Grace Liu, E-005), a unit manager and an approver.

read.heading: Movers and leavers: where control fails
read.body:
Movers and leavers carry the bigger risk, because access that should end does not.

- Leaver E-027, Registered Nurse, emergency department at Kestrel General Hospital (KGH): terminated 2026-08-14, still Enabled 48 days later on 2026-10-01, with 5 permissions including chart access in the Clinical Information System (A-001). Last directory sign-in 2026-08-13, before termination; activity in each system still needs checking. Review AR-004 is overdue.
- Leaver E-014, agency nurse from ClearPath Staffing (V-03): contract ended 2026-08-31, still Enabled 31 days later, with 4 permissions including order entry, which agency nurses should not hold. Her HR status still reads Active, because a contract end is not an HR event. Her reviewer chose Remove on 2026-09-25 (AR-003) and nothing happened.
- Mover E-028: moved from Unit Clerk at Aspen Ridge Hospital to Clinical Analyst at KGH on 2026-08-17. The old row was never closed, and she kept view chart, update bed status and virtual desktop access from the old role. Review AR-006 is dated 2026-08-28, before it was assigned, so it is not valid evidence.
- Vendor E-015 from Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01): privileged, no MFA, no end date, and an excess view chart grant on A-001.

The pattern is the finding: removal depends on someone noticing. HR events do not reach IT, agency and vendor end dates live outside HR, and review decisions are not carried out (issue I-02).

read.heading: Kevin Park's conflict
read.body:
Kestrel's segregation-of-duties (SoD) rule says no one may hold two or more of provision accounts, approve access and administer audit logs on the Identity Directory (A-007). Kevin Park (E-009), Systems Administrator, holds all three:

- provision accounts, granted in 2016 by Marcus Bell (E-002);
- approve access, granted on 2025-11-03 by himself;
- administer audit logs, granted on 2026-02-17 by himself.

Together these let one person approve a request, create the account, and change the record of having done it. No wrongdoing is needed for this to matter: an honest mistake gets no second look, and nobody can prove afterwards what happened. It also concentrates work, which is part of why requests wait.

The conflict shows up elsewhere too. He reviewed his own access (AR-001, decision Keep), which is not independent. He is the manager of vendor engineer E-015 and the reviewer of E-015's access (AR-002, overdue). His own privileged account has no MFA.

Record this as issue I-01, without blame: the process gave one person these rights because nobody else did the work. The fix belongs in Release 2 design: approval to business owners, audit-log administration to security (Sam Okafor, E-020), and re-approval of the self-granted rights through Daniel Osei (E-004). Until then, a compensating control reduces the risk (proposed): a weekly independent review of E-009's changes in the Identity Directory.

read.heading: Draw the map and measure it
read.body:
Put the current state on one page that a clinician, a manager and an auditor can read:

1. Scope: joiner, mover, leaver, agency and vendor access to A-001, the Bed Management System (A-006), the Virtual Desktop Service (A-008) and the dashboards (A-009), all controlled through the Identity Directory (A-007).
2. Swimlanes: requester, service desk, approver, provisioning, HR, agency or vendor.
3. Steps with evidence, and steps still to be timed.
4. Control points: where a control should act (HR event, approval, review, removal) and whether it did.
5. Pain points: waiting, handoffs and reopened requests.
6. Baseline measures, so Release 2 can prove change.

Recompute the headline measure yourself in the Beacon semantic model:

```
Access Requests Within 72h % =
VAR Resolved =
    FILTER (
        FactServiceTicket,
        FactServiceTicket[TicketType] = "Access request"
            && NOT ISBLANK ( FactServiceTicket[ResolutionHours] )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE (
        COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( Resolved, FactServiceTicket[ResolutionHours] <= 72 ) ),
        COUNTROWS ( Resolved )
    )
```

It should return 27.3% (12 of 44). Keep NOT ISBLANK in the Resolved filter, which feeds both the numerator and the denominator: Data Analysis Expressions (DAX) treats a blank as zero in a comparison, so open tickets would otherwise count as resolved within 72 hours. Week 8 reuses this measure, with the same name and code, on the access-governance dashboard. For missed leavers, filter each worker's latest identity row to Enabled accounts whose hr_status is Terminated or whose effective_to is before 2026-10-01. You should find exactly E-014 and E-027.

keyTerms.definition: A picture of how a process really runs today, with steps, roles, times, control points and failures, used as the baseline for redesign.
An account still Enabled after the worker's termination or contract end. At Kestrel on 2026-10-01 there were two: E-014 and E-027.
Splitting sensitive steps such as approving, provisioning and auditing between different people, so no one can complete and hide a sensitive action alone.
A permission a worker holds that their current role does not include, such as a mover's leftover access or an agency nurse's order entry.
A temporary or alternative control that reduces a risk when the preferred control is not yet in place, such as independent review of an administrator's changes.
A process map with one lane per role or team, which makes handoffs, and the waits between them, easy to see.

build.modelAnswer: Control failures (extract). Leaver E-027: terminated 2026-08-14; Enabled on 2026-10-01 (48 days); 5 permissions; AR-004 overdue. Failed control: HR termination did not trigger removal. Leaver E-014: agency contract ended 2026-08-31; Enabled (31 days); 4 permissions including order entry; AR-003 Remove decided 2026-09-25, not carried out. Failed controls: no end-date feed from ClearPath Staffing; review decisions not tracked to completion. SoD, E-009: provision, approve and audit-log rights, two self-granted (issue I-01).

examTips.tip: Domain 5, Identity and Access Management (IAM): missed leavers are a deprovisioning failure. The best answer ties removal to an authoritative trigger such as HR termination or contract end, not to someone noticing.

Domain 1, Security and Risk Management: segregation of duties splits approve, execute and audit. When it cannot be fixed at once, choose a compensating control such as independent review of that person's actions.
Start where you are: observe and measure the current value stream before redesigning. Where data lacks step times, sample real requests rather than guessing.
Business Environment task 4, Remove impediments and manage issues: I-01 and I-02 are happening now, so they need owners and actions now, not only entries in the risk register.

pitfalls: Mapping the process the policy describes instead of the one the tickets and accounts show.
Counting E-028's two rows as two workers, or missing that the mover kept old access.
Presenting the 4.26-day median as waiting time; the tickets do not separate waiting from work.
Framing Kevin Park's conflict as personal misconduct. It is a design failure to fix through roles and controls.

check.q: Why is E-014 a missed leaver when her HR status says Active?
check.a: She is an agency nurse whose contract ended on 2026-08-31 (her effective_to), and her account was still Enabled on 2026-10-01, 31 days later. Agency end dates come from ClearPath Staffing, not HR, so no leaver event fired. Her reviewer also chose Remove on 2026-09-25 (AR-003) and the decision was never carried out.

check.q: What exactly is Kevin Park's segregation-of-duties conflict, and why does it matter even without misconduct?
check.a: On the Identity Directory (A-007) he holds provision accounts, approve access and administer audit logs, and he granted the last two to himself. One person can approve, create and alter the record of access, so mistakes get no independent check and nothing can be proved afterwards. He also reviewed his own access (AR-001) and made 62.6% of all grants.

check.q: Your measure for access requests within 72 hours returns 38.6% instead of 27.3%. What is the likely bug?
check.a: The numerator is counting the 5 open access requests, whose ResolutionHours is blank, because DAX treats blank as zero in ResolutionHours <= 72. That gives 17 of 44. Count the numerator from the same Resolved table, which keeps only rows where NOT ISBLANK ( FactServiceTicket[ResolutionHours] ); the correct result is 12 of 44, 27.3%.
